name: IVF care

items.title: What happens in an IVF cycle
items.body: IVF usually has these steps: medication to help several eggs mature, scans and blood tests to check progress, a trigger injection, egg collection, fertilisation in the laboratory, and transfer of an embryo to the womb. Your clinic sets the exact plan and timing for you.
suggested_questions: What are the steps of IVF?
How long does one cycle take?

items.title: Ovarian stimulation
items.body: During stimulation you take fertility medication, usually by injection, for around ten days to help several eggs mature at once. Your clinic chooses the medication and dose for you and may adjust it after your scans.
suggested_questions: Why do I need injections?
Can my dose change?

items.title: Monitoring scans and blood tests
items.body: While you take stimulation medication, the clinic checks the growth of your follicles with vaginal ultrasound scans and sometimes blood tests. These visits decide when you are ready for the trigger injection.
suggested_questions: What do the scans show?

items.title: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)
items.body: OHSS is a possible reaction to fertility medication. Mild symptoms include bloating and discomfort. Severe abdominal pain, fast weight gain, shortness of breath or passing very little urine need urgent contact with your clinic.
suggested_questions: What are the signs of OHSS?

items.title: Trigger injection and egg collection
items.body: When the follicles are ready, a trigger injection helps the eggs finish maturing. Egg collection is timed from the trigger and is done with a fine needle guided by ultrasound, usually under sedation.
suggested_questions: Why is the trigger timing so exact?
What happens on collection day?

items.title: Fertilisation and embryo development
items.body: After collection, the eggs are mixed with sperm or injected with a single sperm (ICSI). The laboratory checks fertilisation the next day and watches the embryos develop for several days.
suggested_questions: What is ICSI?

items.title: Embryo transfer
items.body: An embryo is placed in the womb through a thin tube. It is usually quick and does not need sedation. Your clinic will discuss how many embryos to transfer; transferring one reduces the risks of a multiple pregnancy.
suggested_questions: How many embryos should be transferred?

items.title: The wait and the pregnancy test
items.body: Your clinic tells you when to take a pregnancy test after transfer. Keep taking any medication your clinic prescribed, such as progesterone, until they tell you to stop.
suggested_questions: When can I test?
Do I keep taking progesterone?

items.title: Eating well before and during IVF
items.body: There is no special IVF diet. General NHS advice for anyone trying to get pregnant is to eat a healthy, balanced diet, aim for a healthy weight, and take a folic acid supplement and vitamin D. Being very underweight or overweight can make it harder to get pregnant. ReproductiveFacts.org notes there is no evidence that normal variations in diet affect fertility for people of a healthy weight with regular periods; the exception is a diet high in mercury (found in some seafood). There is no scientific evidence that supplements improve fertility. Ask your care team before starting any supplement or herbal remedy, and if you have a condition such as diabetes.
suggested_questions: What should I eat during IVF?
Should I take supplements?

items.title: Alcohol, smoking and caffeine during treatment
items.body: NICE advises that the safest approach when trying to get pregnant is not to drink alcohol. Smoking, including passive smoking, is likely to reduce fertility, and support to stop smoking is available. NICE says there is no consistent evidence linking caffeinated drinks (tea, coffee, energy drinks, colas) with fertility problems; ReproductiveFacts.org suggests avoiding heavy caffeine use. Recreational drugs should be avoided. Your clinic may give you its own advice for your treatment.
suggested_questions: Can I drink coffee during IVF?
Does smoking affect IVF?

items.title: Working during fertility treatment
items.body: IVF usually means several clinic appointments, some at short notice, and you may feel unable to work for a short time after egg collection. Tommy's suggests talking to your manager early about flexible working, working from home or using annual leave. Your employer should treat IVF appointments like other medical appointments, and sickness absence caused by treatment like other sick leave. Your clinic can tell you which days in your plan usually need time off.
suggested_questions: Can I keep working during IVF?
Will I need time off after egg collection?

items.title: Emotional support during treatment
items.body: Fertility treatment can be emotionally demanding. In the UK, every HFEA-licensed clinic must offer you the chance to speak to a counsellor before treatment. Support groups and talking to others who have been through treatment can help, and you can also ask your GP about NHS counselling or find an accredited infertility counsellor privately. If you ever feel unable to cope or unsafe, contact your GP, your clinic or emergency services.
suggested_questions: Is there counselling during IVF?
How do I cope with the stress of IVF?

name: IVF medication preparation

items.title: FSH pen
items.body:
What it does
FSH medication helps several follicles grow at the same time.

What to have ready
The pen, a new pen needle, an alcohol swab, your sharps container and your treatment plan.

Your clinic's video
Shown below when your clinic adds it.

Manufacturer instructions
Use the leaflet in the box. It is the reference for your exact device.

Storage
Follow the storage instructions in the box; many pens are kept in the fridge before first use.

When to call your team
If the pen looks damaged, the liquid looks unusual, or you are not sure of your dose.

items.title: Mixing medication
items.body:
What it does
Some medicines come as a powder and liquid that you mix before injecting.

What to have ready
Both vials, the syringe and needles from your clinic, swabs and your sharps container.

Your clinic's video
Shown below when your clinic adds it.

Manufacturer instructions
Use the leaflet in the box. It is the reference for your exact device.

Storage
Store unmixed vials as the box says. Use mixed medication straight away unless your clinic says otherwise.

When to call your team
If the powder does not dissolve, or you are unsure how much to draw up.

items.title: Medication to prevent early ovulation
items.body:
What it does
This medication stops your body releasing eggs before the clinic collects them.

What to have ready
The prefilled syringe or pen, swabs and your sharps container.

Your clinic's video
Shown below when your clinic adds it.

Manufacturer instructions
Use the leaflet in the box. It is the reference for your exact device.

Storage
Follow the box instructions.

When to call your team
If you miss a dose or inject at the wrong time, contact your care team now.

items.title: Trigger injection
items.body:
What it does
The trigger helps the eggs finish maturing so they can be collected. Its timing is set exactly by your clinic.

What to have ready
The trigger medication, needles, swabs, your sharps container and the exact time from your clinic.

Your clinic's video
Shown below when your clinic adds it.

Manufacturer instructions
Use the leaflet in the box. It is the reference for your exact device.

Storage
Follow the box instructions.

When to call your team
If you are unsure of the time, or think you took it at the wrong time, contact your care team now.

items.title: Progesterone
items.body:
What it does
Progesterone supports the lining of the womb after egg collection and embryo transfer. It may be given as a vaginal gel or pessary, or as an injection.

What to have ready
The form your clinic prescribed and your treatment plan.

Your clinic's video
Shown below when your clinic adds it.

Manufacturer instructions
Use the leaflet in the box. It is the reference for your exact device.

Storage
Follow the box instructions.

When to call your team
If you have side effects, or if you are unsure whether to stop or continue progesterone.

items.title: Sharps and disposal
items.body: Put used needles straight into a sharps container. Do not recap needles. Close the container when it is about three quarters full and return it as your clinic or pharmacy explains.

items.title: Travelling with your medication
items.body: Carry your medication in your hand luggage with your prescription or clinic letter. Keep fridge items cool with a cool bag and plan dose times across time zones with your care team.

items.title: Missed or late dose
items.body: If you missed a dose or took it late, contact your care team now. They will tell you what to do. Do not take an extra dose unless your care team tells you to.
suggested_questions: I missed my dose, what now?

name: Egg freezing

items.title: What egg freezing involves
items.body: Egg freezing uses the same first steps as IVF: medication to mature several eggs, monitoring scans and egg collection. The eggs are then frozen by vitrification and stored for later use.
suggested_questions: What does egg freezing involve?

items.title: Age and success
items.body: The chance of a future pregnancy from frozen eggs is higher when eggs are frozen at a younger age. Freezing eggs does not guarantee a future pregnancy.
suggested_questions: Does my age matter?
How many eggs should I freeze?

items.title: Stimulation for egg freezing
items.body: You take stimulation medication for around ten to twelve days and have scans to check how the follicles are growing. Your clinic chooses the medication and dose.

items.title: Egg collection
items.body: Eggs are collected with a fine needle under ultrasound guidance, usually with sedation. Plan to rest for the remainder of the day.

items.title: Freezing and storage
items.body: Mature eggs are frozen quickly by vitrification and stored in liquid nitrogen. Your clinic explains storage consent, renewal and costs.
suggested_questions: How long can my eggs be stored?

items.title: Using your eggs later
items.body: When you want to use them, the eggs are thawed, fertilised in the laboratory and an embryo is transferred, as in IVF. Not every egg survives thawing.
